debtbook.name: The Debt Book
debtbook.giver: Ida Ferris, a moneylender's clerk on Chandlery Row
debtbook.brief: A clerk on Chandlery Row wants to burn the book of debts her master is selling to the Lantern Hall, and needs someone at the door while she does it.

lines.narrate: Ida Ferris is a clerk at a moneylender's on Chandlery Row: twenty-six, ink to the wrist, her hair held up with a pencil. She finds you at the inn and talks very fast and very quietly, without sitting down.

lines.text: My master sells paper to the Lantern Hall. Debts. Folk on the north quay and in the Tanneries who owe him more than they've got. The Hall buys the paper, and then the Hall owns them, and then a clerk comes round being kind.

oneOf.text: The fund bought the Hall's paper and burned it on the quay. I watched. I cried, if you want to know. And the next Monday the Hall came back to my master and bought what he had left. The Tanneries this time. Forty-six names. A new book.
Two hundred and eighty names in one book. My master's copying it out fair for the Hall tonight, so they can collect it in the morning.

lines.text: I keep the key to the strongroom. I'm going to burn the book tonight. The real one. Without it the Hall's copy is only a list; nobody can be made to pay a list. I need someone at the door while I do it, because my master's son sleeps over the shop, and he's large.
Burning a man's books is theft.
Yes. It is. I've thought about that. I'm going to do it anyway.

choices.label: Stand at the strongroom door while she burns it
Ask her whether there is another way than fire

lines.narrate: The strongroom is at the back of the shop, behind an iron door, and the book lies on a lectern inside: a fat ledger bound in red, with a brass clasp. Ida opens it at the first page. Her hands are shaking. She lights a candle.
Upstairs a floorboard creaks. Then the stair.

lines.text: Ida? Who's down there? Who's that at the door?

choices.label: Talk the moneylender's son back up the stairs

lines.narrate: You tell him the truth, or most of it: that Ida is working late, that you are a friend come to walk her home, that it is cold and he should go back to bed. He looks at you for a long time, and at Ida's candle, and at the book.

lines.text: My mother's name is in that book. From before. Dad bought her debt when they married. Did you know that, Ida?
I know.
Burn it, then. I slept through it.

lines.narrate: He goes back up the stairs. Ida burns the book in the strongroom grate, a page at a time. It takes an hour, and she reads every name before it goes in.

He does not go back up. He comes down, large, in his nightshirt, with the poker from the kitchen, and you stand in the door and do not let him past. It is a long, ugly ten minutes before he gives up and goes for the watch.
By the time the watch comes the book is ash in the grate, and Ida is sitting on the strongroom floor with her hands in her lap, waiting for them.

lines.text: I'll tell them it was me. It was me. You held a door.

choices.label: Stand in the door, and do not let him past

lines.narrate: He comes down the stair with a poker and finds you in the strongroom door, and stops on the bottom step, and looks at you, and does the sum. He goes back up. You hear him sit down on his bed, heavily, and stay there.
Ida burns the book in the grate, a page at a time. It takes an hour, and she reads every name before it goes in.

He comes down the stair with a poker and does not stop. It is a long, ugly ten minutes in the doorway before he gives up and goes for the watch, and you have a bruise the shape of the poker on your forearm.
By the time the watch comes the book is ash in the grate, and Ida is sitting on the strongroom floor with her hands in her lap, waiting for them.

lines.text: I'll tell them it was me. It was me. You held a door.

lines.narrate: Ida stops. It is the first time she has stopped since she found you.

lines.text: There's one. I give it back. Page by page, to the people whose names are on them. Then it's theirs to burn, or keep, or frame. It'll take all night, and I'll be out of a place by morning either way.
All night. Every door on the quay. Yes. Let's do that one.

choices.label: Help her take every page back to the name on it

lines.narrate: You take the book out of the strongroom while the moneylender's son sleeps, and you and Ida walk the north quay and the Tanneries until dawn, knocking. She tears each page out at the door and hands it over.

People do different things with them. A net-maker burns hers on the step, there and then. A carter folds his into his hat. An old woman on Rope Lane reads hers twice and gives it back to Ida, and asks her to keep it, because it has her husband's name on it as well as hers, and it is the last thing she has with his name written on it.

lines.text: I'll keep it. I'll keep it safe.

choices.label: Tell her that fire is quicker

mould.name: The Tenth Mould
mould.giver: Rafe and Tilda Coppin, a miner's children
mould.brief: Two miners' children have found a bell-mould the founders never used, in a gallery closed before they were born, and mean to sell it to the Lantern Hall.

lines.narrate: Rafe Coppin is thirteen and his sister Tilda is eleven, and their mother works the north galleries, and they have found something they should not have. They take you to it by a back way, through a gallery closed before either of them was born, with a lamp each and a great deal of whispering.

It is a bell-mould: clay and iron, the height of two men, sitting on a rotten cradle in a chamber cut to fit it, with its core still in it, never poured. The dust on it is a finger thick. Scratched into the iron band round its foot, very small, there is a line of old writing. Five words. Not this way. Ask them all.

oneOf.narrate: Above you, through the rock, you can hear the ten ringing the hour, the small one first.
Above you, through the rock, you can hear the nine ringing the hour by hand, a little ragged. Someone on the ropes is tired.
Above you, through the rock, you can hear the nine ringing the hour, out of time.

lines.text: The Hall's man at the inn says it's the founders' own. He says Merrowgate would give five hundred gold for it, for the front hall of the Lantern Hall, to show people. Five hundred.
Mam's chest is bad from the galleries. Five hundred is the coast, and a house, and her not breathing dust.
We're not stealing it. We found it. Finding isn't stealing.
How bad is her chest, Rafe?
She coughs all night. She says she doesn't.

choices.label: Persuade them the mould belongs to Cinder Fold, and take it to the committee with them

lines.narrate: You tell them what the words on the band mean, as far as anyone knows: that the founders could have cast a tenth and chose not to, and wrote down why. That it is the one thing in Cinder Fold that says no to the Hall in the founders' own hand, and that it would stand in the Hall's front hall with its writing turned to the wall.

Tilda listens. Rafe argues. Then they take you to Agnes Tallis together, and Agnes looks at the mould for a long time, and pays them a finder's fee out of the committee's box: enough for a physician from Highpass for their mother, and the coal for her room all winter.

lines.text: It's not five hundred.
No. It's what we've got. And it's ours, and so's the mould, and so are you.

lines.narrate: Rafe will not hear it. Five hundred is five hundred. In the end Tilda says she will go to the committee whatever her brother does, and he follows her because he will not let her go alone.
Agnes Tallis pays them a finder's fee out of the committee's box. It is not five hundred. Rafe takes it without saying thank you, and then comes back an hour later and says it.

choices.label: Buy it from them yourself, with what you can spare, and give it to the town

lines.narrate: You count out sixty gold on the dusty cradle. It is not five hundred. It is a physician from Highpass, and coal for their mother's room, and Rafe looks at it for a long time before he picks it up.
You give the mould to the committee the same afternoon. Agnes Tallis has it carried up and stood in the old casting hall, where the council sat, with its writing turned outwards.

lines.text: Not this way. Ask them all. I'll ask. I don't know what I'm asking, but I'll ask.

choices.label: Let them sell it: they found it, and their mother is ill

lines.narrate: You tell them it is theirs to sell. The Hall's man pays them five hundred gold at the inn, in front of everyone, and has the mould dug out and carted down the mountain within the week.

Their mother goes to the coast in the spring. By then the mould stands in the front hall of the Lantern Hall in Merrowgate, behind a rope, with a painted card beside it: the founders' own. It stands with its writing to the wall.

lines.text: They needed it. They needed it more than a hall needs a mould. Didn't they?
Yes. And now the Hall has it.

lamps.name: Lamps for the Roofs
lamps.giver: Mags Peller, who keeps the lamps
lamps.brief: Mags Peller's lamp roster has no names for the far roofs. Find her three people who will walk the long planks at night.

oneOf.narrate: Saltwick is empty, its people gone to Vell in the spring, but its lamps are lit. Mags comes back over the ridge every week with six of her lamplighters to keep them lit, so that there is a town for Saltwick to come back to. The mist lies in the lanes under the lamps, flat, waiting.
Saltwick is still on its roofs, and its lamps still burn on every corner all night. Mags has her roster chalked on the slates of the salt-hall roof, a column of names for every stretch of planks.

lines.text: The far roofs. Past the tannery, where the planks are longest. I've nobody for them at night. My lamplighters are on the near roofs until dawn, and the far ones go dark at two, and the white comes up there first.

Three. I need three who'll walk the far planks at night with a hook, from midnight to dawn, all winter. Not lamplighters. I've no time to train lamplighters. People who'll do as they're told and not look down.
Davin's put his name down. I've rubbed it off. He's fifteen, and they're the long planks.

choices.label: Go round and ask who will walk the far planks

oneOf.narrate: You go round Saltwick's people with Mags's slate, asking who will come back over the ridge with her and walk the far planks of the empty town. Two say yes before supper.
You go round the roofs with Mags's slate. Two people say yes before supper.

lines.narrate: Peg Halloran, who is eighty-one, says she has walked those planks since before the tannery was built and does not intend to stop for a little mist. Mags writes her name down without arguing, which Peg says is the first time in sixty years.

Corry Marl, a carter, says yes before you have finished asking. He drove salt for the Commandery the spring after the tide, on the same road, and nobody here knew him then. He has felt it ever since, he says, and has never known what to do about it. He would like to be told what to do about it.
You need a third. Davin's name is on the slate again, in letters a hand high.

choices.label: Leave Davin's name on the slate, and walk the first night with him

lines.narrate: You leave it. Mags looks at it for a long time, and at you, and does not rub it off.

lines.text: First night, you walk it with him. Every plank. And if he looks down once, he's off the roster.

lines.narrate: He does not look down once. At four in the morning, on the longest plank, past the tannery, he stops and relights a lamp the wind has put out, with one turn of the hook, the way his grandmother does it, and checks it, and goes on.

choices.label: Find a third who is not Davin

lines.narrate: You find Ivo Sefton, a widower who has not slept a whole night since the tide took his wife, and who sits up with a candle anyway. He says he might as well be holding a hook as a candle, and that he has always been good at not looking down.
Mags writes his name on the slate. Then she rubs out Davin's, again, and Davin, from the next roof, watches her do it and does not write it back. Not tonight.
You go round every roof again, and nobody else will take the long planks at night. In the end Mags looks at the slate, and at Davin's name on it, and sighs.

lines.text: Fine. Him. I'll walk it with him myself, the first week. If he looks down once, he's off.

lines.narrate: He does not look down once.

roster.name: The Watch Roster
roster.giver: Reeve Aveline, who keeps the roster
roster.brief: Briarwatch is arguing over who walks the night watch on the Briarwood edge, and Pim has put his own name down for every night of the winter.

lines.narrate: The night-watch roster is pinned to Aveline's board outside the inn, under the letters: a sheet for every week of the winter, with a column for each night and a line in each column for every name.
Most of the lines are empty. One name is in every column of every sheet, in letters an inch high: PIM.

lines.text: Every night. All winter. I've rubbed it out four times and he writes it back before I'm home. Tovin says he can't stop him. Tovin means he won't.
And the rest of the village is in the hall every evening, arguing about whose turn it is, while the sheets stay empty. I've run Briarwatch on lists for twenty years. I can't make this one fill.

oneOf.text: There are two thousand people from Vell in the fields, as well, and none of them has been asked. Half the village doesn't want them on the line. Half of them don't want to be on it.
The houses on the Briarwood side say they've walked that edge for two hundred years, and it's the new houses' turn. The new houses say they pay the same tithe and they're a mile from the trees.

lines.text: Come to the hall tonight. They might listen to you. They won't listen to me; I'm the one with the list.

choices.label: Go to the hall that evening

lines.narrate: The hall is half full, which for Briarwatch on a winter evening means everyone who has an opinion. The roster is on the table at the front, with Pim's name all down it.

lines.text: My grandfather walked the edge. My father walked it. I've walked it forty years. My knees are done. I'm not asking for anything except that somebody else take a night.

lines.narrate: Barnaby Fisk is seventy-three and lives in the last house on the Briarwood side, with the trees at the bottom of his garden.

lines.text: And I'll take a night. I'll take two. But not because Barnaby's grandfather walked it. Because it needs walking. Every house the same, and no house first.

lines.narrate: Jem Tullow keeps the new mill on the Ashford road, and his house is a mile from the trees, and he has said this every evening for a fortnight.

lines.text: We're in your fields. Two thousand of us. We've walked a city wall every night of our lives. Give us nights, and stop arguing about whether we're allowed.

lines.narrate: At the back of the hall, Pim is sitting by the door with his coat on, because the watch goes out at dusk and it is nearly dusk.

lines.text: I'm not trying to make a point. I'm awake anyway. I ring the bell at night. I might as well walk the line between the hours.
That's what you say when you're trying to make a point.
It's also what you say when it's true.

choices.label: Ask them to draw the nights by lot, every house in, no house first

lines.narrate: You put a jar on the table and ask every house to put its name in, once, the Briarwood side and the mill road alike, and to draw the winter's nights out of it, a week at a time, in front of everyone.

oneOf.narrate: Greta Danner puts in a name for every tent in the fields. Nobody stops her. Somebody from the Briarwood side moves up the bench to make room for her.
Barnaby Fisk puts his name in first, and then Jem Tullow, and they do not look at each other, and the rest of the hall comes up after them.

lines.narrate: By the end of the evening the sheets are full. Pim's name comes out of the jar for one night in nine, like everyone's. He looks at the sheet for a long time.

lines.text: One night in nine. What do I do with the other eight?
Sleep, Pim. Ring the bell and go to sleep. That's what the other eight are for.

lines.narrate: You put a jar on the table and ask every house to put its name in. Half the hall does. The other half says a jar is how the Commandery chose people, and they will not be chosen by a jar.

In the end Aveline fills the sheets herself, house by house, the way she fills every list, and everyone in the hall is a little angry with her, which she says is how she knows it is fair. Pim's name stays on every third night. He says that will do, for now.

choices.label: Take Pim's name off every night but one, and walk the rest of his nights yourself while you are here

lines.narrate: You rub Pim's name off every night but one, and write your own in the rest, for as long as you are in Briarwatch.

The hall goes quiet. Then Barnaby Fisk gets up, stiffly, and writes his name under yours on the first night, and Jem Tullow writes his under that, and by the end of the evening there are four names in every column.

lines.text: You're going to Vell. You won't be here for most of them.
Then we'll walk them. We've all just put our names down under that one, lad. That's what that was.

lines.narrate: Pim walks the first night with you, the one he kept. Between the hours, on the line at the stream, he tells you he knew he was being foolish, and that he does not know how to stop doing things for everyone.

choices.label: Pay for lamp oil and a hot supper for the watch every night of the winter

lines.narrate: You give Aveline forty gold for lamp oil and a hot supper at the inn for whoever walks the watch, every night of the winter, and ask her to write it at the top of every sheet.
It does not settle the argument. It changes it. By the end of the week people are arguing about whose turn it is to get the supper, and the sheets are full, and Pim's name is on one night in five.

lines.text: I'd have thought better of them if it hadn't taken a supper. I'd have thought worse of them if it hadn't worked.
